summary: The published contract now claims the ambiguous-PUT retry is safe; measured, it is not -- the window is only written after commitAll RETURNS, so the one case the row exists for is the one case it does not cover. Two further majors: an unanswerable replay refuses the whole batch (the outcome the code comment three lines above says it avoids), and the checkpoint pods map now accumulates across every takeover with no eviction.

findings.title: Sequencer's contract claims the ambiguous-PUT retry is safe; MEASURED false
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED, in my own worktree, single leader, single epoch, no takeover, no checkpoint involved. A BinStore whose putIfAbsent lands the object and then throws IOException (the ambiguous case FaultInjectingStore.Faults.ambiguousPut models). LocalSequencer.commitAll(List.of(new CommitRequest("poda","i1",0,"seg/0",{RA:3}))) throws. The caller retries with the byte-identical triple. Result: two durable deltas on the chain, bins/.../0000000000000001.delta carrying seg/0 at firstOffset=0 and bins/.../0000000000000002.delta carrying seg/0 at firstOffset=3 -- 3 records holding two sets of committed offsets, which is I2 and the exact harm backlog-notes names ('a test written from it is GREEN while one set of records holds two sets of committed offsets'). Cause: LocalSequencer.applyFresh calls window.applied(...) only AFTER log.commitAll RETURNS, so an ambiguous commit is never recorded; window.replayOf then classifies the retry as fresh, CommitLog re-PUTs at the same slot, loses to its own landed delta, apply()s it and writes a SECOND one at the next slot. Sequencer.java:46-49 states 'That is the AMBIGUOUS case, not a clean failure: a conditional PUT whose response was lost has still landed. A retry carrying the SAME (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) is safe (M4.10d): it is answered with the offsets that already apply and appends nothing.' Neither documented limit covers this: the retry DID reuse the triple, and there was no takeover and no checkpoint. Sequencer.java:113-116 repeats it on @throws ('Retrying with the same (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) is safe only from M4.10d'). SequencerDedupTest's own class javadoc says 'THE CASE THIS EXISTS FOR IS THE AMBIGUOUS PUT' and every one of its eight fixtures reaches the window through a commitAll that SUCCEEDED first, so none of them touches it. CheckpointWriter.java:56-60 still carries the requirement unchanged and unmet -- 'An AMBIGUOUS commit -- the PUT landed, the response was lost -- applies without ever reaching it, which is why M4.10d must reconcile that case from the chain rather than treating this map as authoritative' -- and this diff leaves that paragraph, and CheckpointWriter.java:50-52's 'NOTHING IN src/main READS EITHER BACK YET -- M4.10d is where a successor folds the uncheckpointed tail into the window', both stale. Fix or retract: either the window is written before the PUT (or CommitLog's lost-race arm answers from the attribution already in the slot it re-reads, which it reads anyway), or the javadoc says the retry is safe only after a commit that RETURNED, which is a far weaker claim than the one shipped.

findings.title: An unanswerable replay refuses the batch and loses the co-batched fresh flush -- the outcome the comment above it says it avoids
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED. poda commits (i1,0,seg/0,3 records) then (i1,1,seg/1,4 records), so its window pointer names the delta carrying seg/1 only and a replay of (i1,0) is permanently unanswerable. Submit the batch {replay (poda,i1,0), fresh (podb,i9,0,seg/b,5 records)}: window.answer(replays) throws IOException BEFORE applyFresh(fresh) runs, the whole batch is refused, and podb's 5 records never land -- the next fresh flush starts at offset 7, not 12. That is precisely what LocalSequencer.java:380-384 says the code does not do ('the batch is NOT refused when one is found ... The fresh submissions commit; the replays are ANSWERED') and what backlog-notes forbids ('Refusing the batch loses the co-batched flush, against Sequencer's "the durable delta carrying every submitted segment"'). It is also PERMANENT: the same request is unanswerable on every retry, and BatchingSequencer.commitBatch (BatchingSequencer.java:384-399) deliberately does not split a failed window, so one pod's poisoned replay fails every window-mate in every window it joins, indefinitely. BatchingSequencer's own comment there -- 'The only in-protocol poison is two submissions sharing a segment key, which the delegate refuses' -- is now false and was not updated by this diff. Reachability today is behind DefaultIngest's unconditional flushSeq++, but this row is where the seam's semantics are DECIDED, and what shipped decides them the way the notes rule out.

findings.title: The checkpoint's pods map now grows with cluster history and nothing evicts
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: six successive terms, each with a distinct ephemeral pod name committing once. Decoded pods per written checkpoint went 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and the encoded body 51 -> 156 bytes (+21/pod at short names; ADR-0036 prices a real slot at ~32 bytes plus the podId). Before this commit a takeover reset CheckpointWriter.pods, bounding the map by pods that committed to the CURRENT leader; inherit()'s putAll makes it cumulative across every term, and nothing anywhere removes an entry. The glossary's ingester is 'K8s pods, 3 AZ, scalable', so pod names churn on every scale event and rolling deploy -- the map therefore grows with cluster history, which is the exact consequence ADR-0036 rejects its qualifier alternative for ('adds a permanent pods entry per restart, so the checkpoint grows with history against ADR-0033') and which its size argument ('Widening the value stays one entry per pod') assumes away. Every checkpoint is TWO PUTs (the .ckpt and the /LATEST pointer) every K deltas or T seconds forever, each carrying the whole accumulated map, and every takeover GETs it. CheckpointTest's 64 KiB bracket already spends ~38 KiB on a 1,600-stream body, leaving room for order-1,000 pods. IdempotencyWindow.byIncarnation (IdempotencyWindow.java:59) is worse in kind: keyed on podId+incarnationId, so it gains a permanent in-process entry per pod RESTART, with no eviction and no cap, for the life of a leader's term. Neither growth is bounded, argued in the diff, or amended into ADR-0036.

findings.title: Six {@link #inherited} references to the method this commit deleted
findings.failure_scenario: ChainReplay.inherited was removed; six javadoc references to it remain in the same file at lines 94, 297, 343, 350, 358 and 361, plus a prose 'the crossing that actually reads the ancestry is `inherited()`' at line 133. Line 94 is the worst: it is the ONLY javadoc on the new crossing(), and it defines the new method entirely by reference to a method that no longer exists ('{@link #inherited}, keeping the pods the walk's checkpoints carried'), so a reader who follows it finds nothing. Invariants.java WAS swept (ChainReplay.inherited -> ChainReplay.crossing) in this same diff, so the omission is in the file the author was editing. No gate catches it -- ChainReplay is package-private and `./gradlew :sequencer:javadoc` (which I ran) does not process it.

findings.title: A third copy of GET-and-decode, against the rule ChainReplay.read's javadoc states
findings.failure_scenario: DeltaReader.at re-implements `try (InputStream in = store.get(key)) { ChainEntry.decode(in.readAllBytes()) }` rather than calling ChainReplay.read(store, key), which exists, is package-private for exactly this purpose, and whose javadoc says in terms: 'PACKAGE-PRIVATE, not private, because ChainEnd reads the one entry it needs through the same decoder. Two copies of "GET it and decode it" is how a reader stops agreeing with its sibling about what a chain entry is.' There are now three (CommitLog.readEntry:168, ChainReplay.read, DeltaReader.at). Concretely: any future change to how a chain entry is fetched -- a range read for the header, a size guard, a retry -- is applied to two of the three and the answering path silently keeps the old behaviour. DeltaReader's own javadoc claims 'The seam is real rather than convenient'; the seam may be, but the duplicated body is not part of it.

findings.title: inherit() mutates pods without synchronized while the ticker thread is already running
findings.failure_scenario: Every other access to CheckpointWriter.pods is inside the monitor: capture() runs under synchronized observe(), writeIfDirty()/writeOnTick() are synchronized. inherit() is not, and it is called from LocalSequencer.start AFTER the CheckpointWriter constructor has already started tickerThread. A tick that fires concurrently with inherit()'s putAll would read a HashMap mid-resize in Map.copyOf(pods). It is safe today only because writeIfDirty returns at `if (!dirty || closed)` and dirty is false until the first capture -- a second field's value doing a lock's job, and an argument the method's javadoc does not make (its '⚠️ ONLY ONCE, BEFORE ANY COMMIT' paragraph argues put-vs-merge, not thread safety). Adding synchronized costs nothing on a once-per-start call.

findings.title: @return still promises 'the durable delta' for a case that now returns a synthesized one
findings.failure_scenario: commitAll's '@return the durable delta carrying every submitted segment' and commit's '@return the durable delta, carrying each run's assigned firstOffset' were left unchanged, while LocalSequencer.commitAll:403 now returns `new CommitDelta(delta.sequence(), merged)` for a mixed batch -- an object that is not any delta in the store: its sequence names the fresh write and its segment list includes replayed segments at offsets that live in a different object. The author flagged this in a code comment at LocalSequencer.java:404-409, but the contract a caller READS still says durable, and this interface's own javadoc is where every other settled attribution question was recorded (see the 'SETTLED BY M4.7b' paragraph). A caller that stores or re-encodes the returned delta -- nothing does today -- writes a delta that never existed.

findings.title: The refusal message states a cause the sequencer cannot distinguish
findings.failure_scenario: The IOException reads '... which the delta at sequence N does not carry; it was consumed by a commit that did not land and its records were never assigned offsets'. The same class's own javadoc four lines earlier says the opposite and is right: 'TWO histories reach this branch and the sequencer cannot tell them apart: a flushSeq consumed by a commit that then threw, and a genuine duplicate whose delta has been superseded.' In the second history the records WERE assigned offsets, and an operator reading this line while debugging a duplicate-records report is told, definitively, that they were not -- sending them to look for lost records instead of duplicated ones. State both histories, or state neither.

findings.title: The fake never refuses, so it hides the real sequencer's refusal rather than the duplication
findings.failure_scenario: FakeSequencer keeps every applied SegmentCommit in an unbounded map forever and answers ANY replayed triple. LocalSequencer answers only when the ONE pointer it keeps per incarnation names a delta carrying the exact triple, and throws IOException otherwise -- the aReplayThePointedDeltaDoesNotCarryIsREFUSED case, which is reachable after a single later flush from the same incarnation. So a caller writing a retry test against the fake sees an answer where production throws: the fake is strictly more permissive, which is the inverse of the divergence the new comment says the fake exists to prevent ('a fake that applied a replay twice would let a caller's retry tests pass'). The comment does disclose 'Kept deliberately SIMPLER than the real one', but simpler here means it cannot produce production's only failure mode. Also FakeSequencer's all-replay path returns `new CommitDelta(nextSequence - 1, answered)` -- the LAST delta's sequence, not the one that holds the answered records -- where LocalSequencer returns window.sequenceOf(replays), the real one.

verified: Item 3 of the brief, cost of inherit(): CONFIRMED zero additional requests. inherit() reads only CommitLog.inheritedPods (a field set by crossFrom off the Crossing the walk already produced) and calls writer.inherit (a putAll). No store call on the path. ChainReplay.crossFromCheckpoint takes the pods off the Checkpoint that CheckpointCursor.newest had already fetched to bound the crossing. BoundedRecoveryCorrectnessTest's exact-cost assertions (18L, and the burned-epochs one) are untouched by the diff and the sequencer suite is green in my tree, so a second CheckpointCursor.newest would have shown up.

Item 6 of the brief, the pods.putAll narrowing: CONFIRMED, both ways. Statically, all three call sites of crossFromCheckpoint return or break on true (ChainReplay.java:135-138, the Continue arm, the neverOpened arm), the three arms of the while body are mutually exclusive per iteration, and replayAncestry is invoked at most once per ChainReplay instance (replay() once, crossing() once behind prevEpoch >= 1). Measured: I instrumented crossFromCheckpoint to throw on a second success AND on any putAll that would clobber a differing slot, and ran the whole :sequencer suite -- green, neither probe fired. The walk cannot consume two checkpoints, so putAll is not a bug.

Item 4 of the brief, the splits: IdempotencyWindow and Submission are real seams. DeltaReader's seam is real but its body duplicates ChainReplay.read -- filed as a minor, not as an objection to the split.

Item 5 of the brief, honesty of the stated limits: the uncheckpointed-tail limit and the DefaultIngest-seam limit are stated accurately in LocalSequencer.inherit and Sequencer's javadoc. What is NOT honest is the sentence between them, which claims the ambiguous-PUT retry is safe -- the blocking finding above.
